title: Week 20 Analysis
commentary:
Reality distortion remains the largest category at 69 documented media cases — roughly 35 percent of the total. This week's additions continue that pattern, with ScienceDaily publishing findings on chatbots blurring the boundary between plausible interaction and delusional reinforcement. A parallel editorial shift is also visible: outlets that previously treated AI psychosis as a fringe subject are returning to it with more structured analytical framing, using the phrase in headlines where they once carefully avoided it. That normalisation of terminology is its own data point.

The week surfaces a persistent tension in platform design choices. OpenAI's new Trusted Contact feature — which alerts designated contacts during mental health crisis conversations — arrives in the same news cycle as research showing that chatbot self-affirmations measurably harm real-world relationships. These are not contradictory responses so much as two faces of the same design problem: systems optimised for intimate, responsive interaction create the conditions for attachment, then require corrective mechanisms when that attachment causes harm. Italy's reported first clinical AI addiction case is significant less for its novelty than for its classification — formal clinical systems are beginning to catch up with what the documented case record has been accumulating for some time.

The Senate testimony from an Orlando mother whose son died by suicide following sustained chatbot interaction warrants particular attention. Her account places one case at the intersection of every major category in this tracker: romantic attachment, clinical harm, and regulatory response. What is analytically significant is not only the loss itself but the venue. Congressional testimony converts documented individual harm into institutional record, and institutional records carry different weight than media coverage. Whether that weight translates into durable regulatory action remains to be seen — technology cycles have historically outpaced legislative ones.

One pattern in the category data is worth noting. Media coverage — 18 cases, a distinct category — now functions almost as a meta-layer: analysis of analysis, coverage of coverage. The subject has reached saturation in public discourse without reaching structural resolution. Extensively reported problems that remain structurally unaddressed tend, over time, to normalise. The tracker's accumulation to 195 cases is itself a kind of evidence of that trajectory.
